name: Violet ray

card.summary: An early-1900s glass-electrode electrotherapy wand marketed for skin, scalp and complexion treatment through gentle high-frequency sparking, now mainly a collectible and vintage-beauty curiosity.
card.note: Regulators pursued US makers from the 1940s-50s over cure-all claims; electrical and ozone hazards apply.

quick.overview:
The violet ray is a small high-frequency device, a compact Tesla-type coil attached to a handle with interchangeable glass electrodes that glow violet when switched on. In the 1920s and 30s it was sold for home use, with face, scalp and skin treatments among its advertised uses, for a brighter complexion and healthier-looking hair.

Today it is mostly seen in antique markets and in some vintage-beauty circles. Early medical commentary, a 1917 JAMA editorial and mid-century US enforcement actions criticised the broad health claims, and no modern trial has tested it for skin or hair appearance.
quick.how: Historically, the user moved the glass electrode over the skin or scalp, and different electrode shapes were meant for face, scalp or body areas. Period manuals recommended treatment sessions on a regular basis, and the glow and tingling were part of the appeal.
quick.risks: The device produces ozone and high-voltage sparks, and old units can have damaged insulation or aged wiring. Burns and electric shock are possible, and the US effectively ended domestic manufacture after FDA actions in the 1940s and 1950s. Medical commentators describe it as an example of discredited electrotherapy.

lead: A violet ray is an antique electrotherapy device that delivers high-voltage, high-frequency, low-current electricity through a handheld glass electrode, producing a violet glow and a faint smell of ozone [1][2]. It descends from high-frequency work associated with Nikola Tesla and the French physicians Jacques-Arsene d'Arsonval and Paul Oudin [3].

Manufacturers including Renulife, Fitzgerald and Fisher sold units to households before the Depression, advertising uses from back pain to skin and scalp complaints. For appearance, adverts promised a glowing complexion, clearer skin and stimulation of the scalp for hair, and period manuals described passing the electrode over these areas [1][2].

The devices drew early criticism. A JAMA editorial in 1917 questioned claims that the apparatus could treat nearly everything, and US makers faced seizures and lawsuits from the 1940s, ending with the 1951 prosecution of Master Electric of Marion, Indiana [1][3].

chain: Glass electrode passed over skin or scalp
Small sparks and ozone produced at the surface
Marketed as stimulating circulation and clearing skin
Claimed brighter complexion and healthier hair
angle.text: Advertising from the 1920s onward presented the violet ray as a way to stimulate skin and scalp for a clearer complexion and better hair. The effect is a claim made by manufacturers; the device does not emit real ultraviolet treatment light in the manner its name implies.

paras: A control box houses the interrupter and coil; a Bakelite handle with a high-voltage coil carries a port for evacuated glass electrodes in different shapes, so the glow can be applied to different parts of the body [1]. The violet colour comes from gas discharge in the electrode and is not actual therapeutic ultraviolet radiation [3].

High-frequency currents were studied by Tesla, d'Arsonval and Oudin in the 1890s, and a JAMA Dermatology historical article discusses Tesla's connection to the violet ray [4]. The device became a consumer product in the 1910s and 20s, with a 1917 dental journal piece describing how practitioners explained its effects [3][5].

The 1940s and 1950s saw recalls, seizures and prosecutions of makers; several manufacturers also stopped during World War II to build radio coils. Master Electric, the last US manufacturer, pleaded guilty in 1951 and was fined $2,000 [1].

Claims ranged from lower back pain to nasal catarrh and 'brain fog' [1]. Edgar Cayce recommended it in almost 900 readings [1]. Skin, scalp and hair uses appear in advertising from the period, such as the ads preserved in vintage-advertising collections [6].
Antique units are collected and sold at markets. Since the 1990s, similar 'violet wands' have been marketed for other forms of electrostimulation [1].

No studies found. Early twentieth-century literature includes practitioners' reports on high-frequency apparatus [5], but no modern controlled trial has tested a violet ray for skin or hair appearance.

timeline.event: Paul Oudin develops a high-frequency apparatus for medical use [3].
JAMA editors question claims that violet-ray apparatus can treat nearly any condition [3].
Master Electric, the last US maker, pleads guilty and is fined [1].

lore.intro: Violet rays are discussed mostly as vintage quack-medicine curiosities and collectible gear.

claims.claim: The violet ray improves complexion and hair by stimulating circulation
claims.believers: 1920s adverts and manuals told users that the glow stimulated the skin and scalp [1][6].
claims.experts: Mid-century US regulators found the health claims unsupported, and no trials examine appearance outcomes [1].
